strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel two-part methodology: (1) an unsupervised, principled SAE-based approach (small dictionary, Top-K) for discovering interpretable reasoning taxonomies without top-down assumptions, and (2) 'constructive model diffing', which moves beyond post-hoc feature attribution (e.g. crosscoders) by explicitly reconstructing the base-to-thinking diff and measuring recovered performance—an elegant and testable operationalization of the 'mechanism vs. heuristic' hypothesis.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: nine base/thinking pairs spanning 0.5B-32B, three benchmarks (including a held-out Hendrycks-MATH split disjoint from training/MATH500), and consistent qualitative/quantitative agreement between two independent measurements (category-vector training loss and hybrid recovery %).

Rigorous ablation studies (random category, random vectors, MLP-magnitude-only, random positions) that convincingly rule out trivial explanations (e.g., that steering merely biases toward specific tokens/answers) and isolate which components of the construction carry the causal signal.

Careful validation of the LLM-based evaluation pipeline against human annotators (κ=0.88 for benchmark grading, and separate validation of taxonomy category labels and judges), which substantially strengthens confidence in the automated metrics used throughout.

Strong attention to reproducibility and controls: disjoint train/val/test splits, best-of-three selection via a held-out 'holdout mix' never used for benchmark reporting, detailed appendices with exact prompts/hyperparameters, seed-stability analysis of the SAEs, and a public codebase.

The finding itself (RL orchestrates pre-existing mechanisms while SFT-distillation installs new ones) is novel, non-obvious, and has clear practical implications for efficient reasoning-model development, tying together several strands of prior work (latent reasoning in base models, taxonomy studies, steering) into a unifying causal account.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation ('RL teaches heuristics over existing mechanisms; SFT installs new mechanisms') is inferred indirectly from differential recovery rates; the paper does not fully rule out alternative explanations, e.g., that category-vector optimization is simply easier when the student and teacher share the same base model/training distribution (as in ORZ, self-generated data) versus when the student imitates an externally distilled teacher (R1-Distill) with a different token distribution—a distributional-shift confound that is related to but not identical to the mechanism/heuristic distinction claimed.

The steering pipeline's coefficient MLP is trained jointly using thinking-model next-token signal, so although the paper argues persuasively (and partly demonstrates via ablation) that direction selection is more causally important than magnitude, the heuristic and mechanism components are not perfectly disentangled, as acknowledged in the limitations.

The discovered taxonomies are acknowledged to be biased toward mathematical/computational reasoning (since evaluation and training data are largely math-focused), which limits confidence that the 'RL teaches when, SFT teaches what' conclusion generalizes beyond mathematical reasoning to other domains (coding, open-ended reasoning, etc.).

Only a single mixed SFT+RL model (QwQ-32B) is examined, limiting the generality of claims about mixed-paradigm training; additionally only one RL-trained model family (Open-Reasoner-Zero) and one SFT-distilled family (DeepSeek-R1-Distill) are studied, so the RL vs. SFT distinction could partly reflect idiosyncrasies of these specific model families/training recipes rather than the paradigms in general.

The pipeline has many interacting moving parts (SAE taxonomy selection via grid search, category-vector optimization, heuristic extraction, best-of-three run selection) that, while each individually well-documented, together create a complex system where compounding hyperparameter choices could affect the magnitude (though probably not the qualitative direction) of the reported recovery percentages, making exact independent replication nontrivial despite the released code.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important question in the reasoning-model literature: whether thinking models acquire genuinely new capabilities through RL/distillation or primarily learn to orchestrate pre-existing base-model competencies.

The unsupervised, bottom-up SAE clustering methodology for discovering interpretable reasoning categories is a methodologically interesting alternative to manual or LLM-derived taxonomies used in prior work (e.g., Gandhi et al.), and the paper provides a systematic three-part evaluation (completeness, consistency, independence) with a principled grid search over layers/cluster sizes.

The hybrid-model experiment is evaluated across a reasonably diverse set of base/thinking model pairs (three base model families, four thinking models including both distilled and RLVR-trained QwQ-32B) and two benchmarks of differing difficulty (GSM8K, MATH500), which supports some generalizability of the qualitative trend.

The ablation studies (only-bias, random-firing, random-vectors) are well-designed and directly test the paper's central claim: showing that both correct timing and specific learned directions are necessary for the hybrid model's gains, lending some causal support to the 'when vs. how' framing.

Reproducibility efforts are strong: detailed appendices document SAE training hyperparameters, steering vector optimization procedures, prompts for the taxonomy evaluation pipeline, and a public code/demo release.
The qualitative example (Figure 3) and steering-usage statistics in the appendix add some interpretability and transparency about which reasoning mechanisms are invoked and how often.
weaknesses: The central 'when not how' narrative is potentially confounded by the hybrid model's generation procedure: at each token, the method searches over 10 coefficients × 5 windows and selects the completion with lowest perplexity under the *target thinking model*. This gives the thinking model oracle-like access to select not just when to steer but effectively which specific steered continuation to keep, which goes beyond a pure 'timing' signal and may leak more thinking-model information into the base model's outputs than the framing suggests.

Steering vectors are optimized by directly maximizing likelihood of the thinking model's actual rollout completions (via gradient-based training), which is itself a form of targeted training/distillation on thinking-model outputs, even though the base model's weights remain frozen. The paper's repeated claim of 'no weight updates'/'no training' is technically true for the base model but somewhat obscures the fact that substantial optimization against thinking-model targets is happening elsewhere in the pipeline.

Results are highly uneven across model scale: for the smallest base model (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B) gap recovery is 0% on GSM8K (hybrid model actually performs *worse* than the base model), and the no-sweep results in the appendix (Tables 4-5) show multiple configurations with negative gap recovery, undermining the generality of the headline 91%/81.8% recovery numbers, which appear cherry-picked from the most favorable (largest) models and the most extensive hyperparameter sweep.

The extensive per-token hyperparameter sweep required to achieve strong results (used for larger models) is computationally expensive and requires repeated queries to the thinking model during generation; this is not clearly acknowledged as a limitation, and the paper does not report compute cost or discuss whether this undermines the practical 'efficiency' claims made in the introduction/conclusion about efficient training implications.

The taxonomy evaluation metrics (completeness, consistency, independence) all rely on LLM-as-judge scoring with GPT-4.1-mini/o4-mini, and the paper explicitly notes 'the alignment between our evaluation pipeline and true human judgment remains to be validated'—no human validation study is provided despite interpretability being one of the three stated goals of the taxonomy.

The RLVR causal claim in the abstract/conclusion is drawn largely from experiments dominated by distilled models (SFT on R1 outputs), with only one genuinely RLVR-trained model (QwQ-32B) tested; generalizing the 'RLVR teaches when, not how' conclusion primarily from distillation-based models is a stretch that is not fully addressed.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting is given for the main hybrid-model results, and it is unclear how sensitive the reported gap-recovery percentages are to the discrete SAE cluster count, layer choice, or random sampling of training sentences.

The paper's contribution is largely empirical/demonstrative; while interesting, some claims in the conclusion (e.g., implications for 'more efficient training of reasoning,' explaining why distillation is effective) are speculative extrapolations not directly tested by the experiments presented.
